Monsters use the same rules as heroes, attributes, skills, and W/S/S damage. If you can read a character sheet, you can read a stat block. The only difference is that monsters don't level up, don't have DP, and don't roll to survive. When they hit 0 HP, they're done.

#pagebreak()

== Reading a Stat Block

#figure(align(center)[#table(
  columns: (35.00%, 65.00%),
  align: (auto, auto,),
  table.header([Field], [Description],),
  [*Name*], [Creature type and challenge rating],
  [*Attributes*], [B/F/A/G/K/R modifiers, from -2 to +2. Most monsters have 0s in the attributes they don't use, so a block lists only the ones it does use and finishes with *others +0*. A block with no Attributes line uses +0 in every attribute.],
  [*HP*], [Health points. When this hits 0, the creature is defeated. The printed figure is the group rate: three rounds of one attacker, which is what a creature standing in a field of five faces. A block the party may meet on its own prints its solo figure beside that number, sized for four attackers, and that is the one to use when the creature fights the whole party alone.],
  [*DR*], [Damage reduction. Subtract from physical damage just like hero armor.],
  [*Attacks*], [W/S/S damage per attack. Weak/Standard/Strong values.],
  [*Multiattack*], [The creature's attack routine: every attack named on the line is made as one action, so a creature with this line spends its action on all of them rather than on one. A block that prints no Multiattack line attacks once.],
  [*Recharge*], [A one-per-encounter ability that may return. At the start of the monster's turn, a player rolls 1d6; on a 5-6, the ability is ready again.],
  [*Abilities*], [Special powers. These override the normal rules, the stat block always wins.],
)], kind: table, numbering: none, outlined: false)

*The block says what it can do, not what it wants.* Its target is your call, and its abilities are the tactics to make that call with: a Recharge line, a Multiattack or a condition on a hit is the turn the creature was built for, so give it room to take it. When the fight turns, it checks morale like any other creature (@sec-morale), unless its block prints its own Morale clause, which overrides that default.

== Creating Monsters

Assign attributes (-2 to +2), give 1–3 attacks with W/S/S damage per the damage budget (@sec-damage-budget), add 1–2 abilities. HP = 3 × (your tier's band average minus its DR), rounded to the nearest whole number; the band average is 5.67 at Novice, 7.50 at Adept, and 9.59 at Master, being that tier's three values weighted by the 3d6 odds (56 in 216 Weak, 140 in 216 Standard, 20 in 216 Strong). Those three rounds are counted per attacker, so multiply the result by the number of attackers the creature faces each round: about one for a creature standing in a group, one per hero for a creature that fights the party alone. DR cannot exceed your tier's ceiling: 3 at Novice, 4 at Adept, 6 at Master. Adjust to taste; printed monsters are hand-tuned.

*Quick Monster Template:*

+ Choose type (Beast, Undead, etc.)
+ Set Challenge (1/2–12)
+ HP = 3 × (your tier's band average minus its DR), counted per attacker (about one in a group, one per hero for a creature that fights the party alone), rounded to the nearest whole number; DR cannot exceed your tier's ceiling (3 at Novice, 4 at Adept, 6 at Master), adjust to taste
+ Choose 1–2 attacks with W/S/S damage per the damage budget, scaled by Challenge:
  + C1–2 (Novice): W:4 / S:6 / St:8
  + C3–6 (Adept): W:5 / S:8 / St:11
  + C7+ (Master): W:7 / S:10 / St:14
+ Add 1 signature ability from its type

#callout(type: "note", title: "Adjusting Monster Difficulty On the Fly", body: [
The stat block is a starting point, not a contract. If a fight is too easy or too hard, change it. The players can't see the numbers.

*Too easy?* The monster has a second phase. When it drops to 0 HP, it roars, gains 10 HP, and its damage tier increases by one. The cultist leader drinks a potion. The wolf pack's alpha arrives, drawn by the sounds of combat. You're not cheating, you're making the fight interesting.

*Too hard?* The monster is wounded from a previous fight. Reduce its HP by 25%. Remove its Multiattack, it's favoring an injured limb. Its Recharge ability doesn't recharge, it used it earlier today on a different party of adventurers. The monster wants to survive too, it might flee at half HP instead of fighting to the death.

*The golden rule:* Adjust in the fiction, not the math. Don't say "I'm reducing its HP by 10." Say "You notice a deep wound in its flank, someone fought this thing before you. It's already bleeding." The players feel smart for noticing. They don't need to know you just turned a Deadly encounter into a Hard one.

*Morale is your best tool.* If the party is getting crushed and the fight was supposed to be Standard difficulty, the monsters get overconfident. One stops to gloat. Another starts looting a downed hero instead of finishing them. The monsters make mistakes, and mistakes give the party openings. This isn't pulling punches. It's playing the monsters like they're alive.
])
